children: Google announced its newest artificial-intelligence model Wednesday, sending the tech giant's stock higher as it attempts to keep up with rivals in the race to build powerful AI models.
Google is rolling out the new model, dubbed Gemini 4 Argon, to a set of cybersecurity companies before making it available to developers, customers, and consumers at a later date.

"Teams are using it extensively at Google, from coding to quantum computing," CEO Sundar Pichai wrote of Argon in a pair of social media posts. "We're going to make it available as soon as we can and as safely as we can."

Shares of Google parent Alphabet rose 1.6% after hours. The stock gained 0.9% in regular trading-and was up as much as 3.4% earlier in the afternoon, according to Dow Jones Market Data, before the broader market dipped just ahead of the closing bell.

The release of Argon indicates Google intends to stay at the cutting edge of AI development. An apparent delay in model releases, the departure of star AI researchers, and poor results in AI benchmarks had sparked worries among investors and analysts that DeepMind-the company's AI research lab-was lagging behind its rivals.

Argon isn't a cure-all for those concerns, but it is a start. Google said that in the company's internal testing, the model outperformed flagship models from OpenAI and Anthropic in various tasks related to knowledge work, coding, science and math, and cybersecurity.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Google will launch Argon at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Tokens are the measurement for the size of an AI query.

That token price is half the cost of Anthropic's most powerful model, Claude Opus 5.5, and a fifth of the price of OpenAI's leading GPT-6 Astra model. It isn't clear how long the introductory price will last or what the base price will be.

The phased rollout-first to cybersecurity partners and then to the general public-reflects the debates about model safety that have gripped the AI industry. After a meeting at the White House on Wednesday, Pichai and other industry executives signed a statement committing to voluntary internal AI safety controls and external reviews.
Google said in a blog post that the company would continue to gather feedback from test users and improve guardrails for the model.
